report:
## Conclusion: Yes — denosumab significantly reduces vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis

The evidence strongly supports this conclusion, based on high-quality randomized controlled trial data.

**Key evidence: The FREEDOM Trial**

The pivotal trial establishing this effect is FREEDOM (Fracture REduction Evaluation of Denosumab in Osteoporosis every 6 Months), a large, international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study involving 7,868 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (denosumab 60 mg vs. placebo, every 6 months for 3 years). Published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, the trial found that new radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in only 2.3% of the denosumab group versus 7.2% of the placebo group — a relative risk reduction of approximately 68% (risk ratio 0.32; 95% CI 0.26–0.41; P<0.001) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0809493; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19671655/). The trial also showed reductions in nonvertebral and hip fractures, alongside increases in bone mineral density at the spine and hip.

**Durability of effect**

Long-term follow-up data from the FREEDOM Extension study (up to 10 years of continuous denosumab treatment) confirm that fracture risk reduction and BMD gains are sustained with ongoing therapy (https://www.drugs.com/monograph/denosumab.html?references=1). Similar efficacy has been replicated in other populations, including a Japanese cohort, which found a 65.7% reduction in new/worsening vertebral fractures (hazard ratio 0.343) (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/268786278).

**Caveats**
Benefits require continued dosing — discontinuation is associated with rapid bone loss and rebound vertebral fracture risk, so treatment continuity or transition planning is clinically important.

**Bottom line:** Robust RCT evidence (FREEDOM and its extension) confirms denosumab meaningfully reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal osteoporosis, supporting a "yes" answer.
